![07-tilt-gravity](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/R7nIII549ICPnqm2m1FpXVoeyFfOb41u/9722306299e63c59c464ca9895db58c8079d25f5195968ea1eda3288b63b9304.png)

This review focused on whether an 8 mm marble has an unobstructed path into and out of the existing LoopLift rotor. The source geometry was inspected in section, and fresh sphere–solid intersections were run along the lower inlet and upper outlet with the rotor held at the correct index. The 90 inlet positions and 70 outlet positions reported no overlap for a 3.98 mm-radius test sphere.

That result is narrower than saying the lift works. A separate alignment sweep showed how quickly the pocket begins to interfere when the rotor moves away from the loading position. The nominal centred angular clearance is about ±0.88 degrees. The gravity study also shows that a steep rotor gives a comparatively small gravity component along the axle. Loading while turning, friction and release timing still need testing.

The concrete output is a set of true CAD sections, two clearance plots, an alignment plot and a tilt study. No physical marble cycle was tested, and no machine geometry was changed in this pack. The next work is to review the loading window and test the inlet with one ball before adding more.

This review examined the drive interfaces rather than only the overall assembly. The shaft, bushes, rotor, guards, spacer and crank were mapped along the axle. The stack drawing makes gaps visible that still require a real fastener-stack review; the existing assembly is not treated as proof that the retainer hardware is correct.

A fresh 5-degree sweep compared 22 mm, 28 mm and 36 mm crank radii. The 36 mm version interfered with nearby inlet/return geometry. Neither the 22 mm baseline nor the 28 mm candidate showed overlap at the sampled angles. The published machine remains at 22 mm; the larger candidate is not being called approved.

Separate sensitivity calculations examined bore/shaft errors, ball diameter versus pocket diameter, and how rotor thickness consumes the nominal face gaps. Those error values are scenarios, not measurements of a printer. An expanded eight-hole clearance coupon was generated as STEP and STL and checked as a watertight single solid. It has not been printed. The next step is measuring the actual ball and checking the coupon before committing to interface dimensions.

![07-relief-comparison](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/R7nIII549ICPnqm2m1FpXVoeyFfOb41u/eff0b5963980834a0bebf590a3ec4f2a0980bb4d1d186cfc41f712331ba27254.png)

This review extended the previous straight-track checks to the transfer regions. The three route segments were mapped in plan and height, then each corner was screened with an ideal rolling-speed and no-wall-hit projectile model. The model projected landing-centre offsets of about 21.6 mm and 19.5 mm. The nominal centre-safe radius of the receiving cup is 4.5 mm. This flags transfer risk; it is not proof that a ball escapes because the simplified model excludes rim impacts, friction and other contact effects.

An exact geometric sweep of the last track centreline and its extension found a different, concrete problem: the test sphere intersected the inlet funnel lip, with maximum overlap around 9.00 mm³. The earlier report had sampled only interior straight-track positions and did not establish this interface was clear.

Two separate lip-relief candidates were generated. The first reduced the collision but left a maximum sampled overlap of 2.68 mm³. Extending the clearance cut removed 37.55 mm³ of funnel material and reduced sampled overlap to 0.000 mm³. The candidate remains separate from the published machine: wall strength, retention and real capture behaviour are untested. The next step is a one-interface print and slow single-ball test, not an immediate claim of a working loop.

This review audited the published manufacturing outputs and separated what they prove from what remains untested. The 21 print-part mesh records were checked for single-body topology, watertightness and bed placement. The stored generic PrusaSlicer results were then broken down by footprint, height, filament volume and estimated print time. These are existing computational reports being reviewed, not new physical prints.

The baseplate and rotor account for much of the material, while the taller stands need separate attention to adhesion, support removal and stiffness. The fit coupon should be printed before the complete machine. Machine print-time estimates were deliberately kept separate from participant work time.

A verification matrix distinguishes export/geometry checks, the fresh nominal-path audit, the newly found funnel interference, idealised corner screening and missing physical evidence. A prospective seven-stage physical test sequence was prepared, covering measurement, empty rotation, loading, discharge, individual corners, funnel return and repeated full cycles. No stage was marked physically complete. Hardware purchasing and print-ready release remain dependent on those checks.
